# 10 Employee Welcome Kit Ideas for Indian Companies (2026)

# 10 Employee Welcome Kit Ideas for Indian Companies (2026)

I have packed a lot of welcome kits. Not the branded backpack kind, the food kind, for companies who wanted a new joinee's first morning to feel like somebody actually thought about it. And the thing I keep noticing is that most employee welcome kit ideas in India come from merchandise vendors, so every list looks the same. Notebook, bottle, lanyard, tote bag, done.

The problem with that list is that it assumes a new joinee wants more stuff. Most of them already own a bottle. What they do not have on day one is a desk drawer with anything edible in it, a reason to talk to the person sitting next to them, or any sense of what this company is like when nobody is presenting a slide about culture.

So this is my version of the list. Ten ideas, drawn from kits we have actually built for teams at Zepto, Dr. Reddy's and a few Pune startups nobody has heard of yet. Some of them involve food, because that is the business I run. Several do not. I have put rough costs against each one because a list without numbers is not much use to an HR manager with a per-head budget.

## What a welcome kit is actually for

Before the ideas, the frame. A welcome kit has one job on day one and a different job in week three.

On day one it signals effort. A new joinee walks in slightly nervous, and the kit on their desk is the first physical evidence that somebody knew they were coming. That is the whole trick. A ₹400 kit that arrived on time beats a ₹2,000 kit that shows up on Thursday.

By week three the branded notebook is in a drawer and the tote bag is being used for groceries. What survives is whatever the person consumes or uses daily. This is why I push clients towards a smaller number of things people actually reach for, rather than a large box that photographs well for the LinkedIn post. The LinkedIn post is a nice side effect. It is not the point.

## 1\. A stocked snack drawer starter, not a snack "hamper"

The difference matters. A hamper is a single event. A starter is four or five single-serve packs that a new joinee keeps in their drawer and finishes over the first fortnight, which is precisely the window where they are skipping lunch because they do not yet know where people eat.

We build these from [Quick Bites](https://thegourmetstories.com/collections/quick-bites), our 25g single-serve range. Salted Cashews and Salted Caramel Almonds are the two that disappear fastest. Cost lands between ₹150 and ₹300 per person depending on how many packs go in, which is well under what most companies spend on the bag alone.

## 2\. A handwritten note from the actual manager

Free. Consistently the thing people mention six months later. Not a printed letter from the CEO with a scanned signature, which everybody can tell is a template. Four lines from the person they will report to, referencing something specific from the interview.

The reason this works is that it cannot be faked at scale, and new joinees know it. If your company hires forty people a month this becomes genuinely hard, and that is fine. Do it for the first thirty days of hires and see whether anyone notices. They will.

## 3\. A desk plant that survives neglect

Money plant, snake plant, jade. Around ₹200 to ₹400 with a decent pot. The failure mode is picking something that needs attention, because a new joinee travelling for training in week two will come back to a dead plant, which is a strange thing to hand someone.

## 4\. A team map instead of an org chart

An org chart tells a new joinee who reports to whom. A team map tells them who to ask about what, who has been here longest, and who knows how the expense system works. Print it, put it in the kit, and it will get referred to more than the employee handbook.

## 5\. Lunch credit for the first week

A ₹1,000 food delivery voucher, or better, a signed chit that says a specific colleague will take them out for lunch on day two. The second version costs nothing and does more. Loneliness in week one is the actual retention risk in the first ninety days, and no notebook fixes it.

## 6\. Something for the family

This is the one Indian companies underuse. A new job is a household event. A small box of [flavoured dry fruits](https://thegourmetstories.com/collections/flavoured-dry-fruits) addressed to the family, not the employee, does something that a branded hoodie cannot. We have shipped these for finance and consulting clients where the new joinee is moving cities and the parents are anxious about it.

Budget ₹500 to ₹900. Send it to the home address, timed for the joining date.

## 7\. A day-one schedule that is actually filled in

Not "10:00 Orientation, 14:00 IT Setup, rest of day free." A filled schedule with names attached. Free to produce, and it removes the worst part of day one, which is sitting at a desk with a laptop that is not provisioned yet and nobody to ask.

## 8\. Good coffee or tea, in a quantity that runs out

A small pack of decent filter coffee or a tin of loose leaf. Around ₹300. The reason it works is that it runs out, and when it does the person goes and finds where the office keeps the good stuff, which is a small excuse to talk to someone. Anything that manufactures a reason to leave your desk in week one is doing useful work.

## 9\. A wellness item people do not already own

Skip the water bottle. Everyone has four. A laptop stand, a decent mousepad, blue-light glasses, or a small pack of [trail mix](https://thegourmetstories.com/collections/superfoods) for the 4pm dip are all in the ₹400 to ₹900 range and none of them are already sitting in a cupboard at home.

Our [Daily Dose and Sports Mix](https://thegourmetstories.com/collections/healthy-snacking) both work here, though I will admit I am not a neutral party on that one.

## 10\. Packaging that does not embarrass anyone

The last idea is not an item. It is the box. I have seen ₹2,500 of good contents arrive in a carton that had clearly been reused, and the whole thing read as an afterthought.

Kraft paper, a belly band with the company mark, tissue that is not creased. On volumes above 250 units a custom sleeve costs ₹30 to ₹80 per box, which is the cheapest quality signal available to you. Below 250 units, a good stock box with a printed sticker gets you most of the way.

## How to put the budget together

Three tiers, based on what I actually see companies spend per new joinee in India right now.

Under ₹800 buys you a snack starter, a handwritten note, a filled day-one schedule and decent packaging. That combination performs better than most ₹2,000 kits because every rupee is in something consumable or useful.

Between ₹800 and ₹1,800 you can add the family box, a plant and a wellness item. This is the band where most mid-size Indian companies land and it is comfortable.

Above ₹1,800 you are into laptop sleeves, premium backpacks and tech accessories, and at that point you should ask whether the money would do more as a joining bonus. Sometimes yes. For senior hires, where the kit is partly a status signal to the rest of the team, no.

One practical note on lead time. Custom packaging needs two to three weeks. Food items need to be ordered against a joining calendar, not held in a cupboard for four months, because the whole point of nuts is that they are fresh. If your hiring is lumpy, order in monthly batches rather than one annual buy.

## Where we come into this

We build the food component of welcome kits for companies across Pune, Mumbai and Bengaluru, usually as a repeating monthly order tied to a joining calendar. Minimums are lower than most people assume and we will do a single sample kit before you commit to anything.

If you want to see the range, start with our [gift boxes](https://thegourmetstories.com/collections/gift-box) for the family component and [Quick Bites](https://thegourmetstories.com/collections/quick-bites) for the desk starter. If you would rather talk to a person about volumes and custom sleeves, our [B2B page](https://thegourmetstories.com/pages/business-gifts) has the details and someone will actually reply.

## Frequently asked questions

**What should an employee welcome kit in India cost per person?**

Most Indian companies spend between ₹800 and ₹1,800 per new joinee. Under ₹800 you can still build a good kit if you spend it on consumables and presentation rather than a large box of branded merchandise. Above ₹1,800 the returns flatten quickly unless the hire is senior and the kit is partly a signal to the wider team.

**When should the welcome kit reach the new joinee?**

On the desk before they arrive on day one, or at the home address two days before joining if they are remote. A kit that arrives in week two reads as an afterthought and loses most of its effect. Work backwards from the joining date and allow two to three weeks if you are using custom printed packaging.

**Are food items a safe choice for a welcome kit?**

Generally yes, provided you check for nut allergies in the joining form and have a non-nut alternative ready. Sealed single-serve packs are safer than open hampers because they travel better and carry clear labels. Avoid anything with a short shelf life if the kit might sit at reception for a few days.

**Should welcome kits be branded with the company logo?**

Light branding on the outer packaging works well. Heavy branding on every item inside makes the kit feel like leftover marketing stock. A printed sleeve or belly band on the box, and unbranded contents, is the combination that consistently gets the better reaction.

**Can we order welcome kits in small monthly batches?**

Yes, and for food-based kits you should. Ordering monthly against your joining calendar keeps the contents fresh and avoids paying for stock that sits in a cupboard. Most suppliers, including us, will run a lower minimum for a repeating monthly order than for a one-time bulk purchase.
